query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, degradation at high temperatures is governed by locally accelerated grain‐boundary diffusion of Ti relative to Cr and other slower‐diffusing elements. This leads to the early formation of discontinuous, Ti‐rich (TiO2) islands along grain boundaries that disrupt the otherwise protective Cr/Al oxide scale. In oxidizing gases, these TiO2 clusters lead to scale inhomogeneity and spallation, whereas in reducing gases, the suppressed formation of continuous Cr2O3/Al2O3 scales results in pronounced internal oxidation along the grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy retaining a single FCC matrix with the inherent microstructural heterogeneity (nonuniform grain-boundary distribution and minor elemental segregation) typical of additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to isothermal treatments at elevated temperatures (e.g., 850–1000 °C) in controlled atmospheres: one set in an oxygen‐rich (oxidizing) environment and another in a gas mixture with reducing characteristics (e.g., diluted H2 in Ar). Additionally, a subset with post‐processing annealing designed to reduce grain-boundary segregation will be compared to the as-printed microstructure.
generation.conditions: Extended exposure (e.g., 100 hours) under fixed temperature and controlled partial pressures of oxygen (for oxidizing conditions) and hydrogen-containing mixtures (for reducing conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary networks that act as fast diffusion pathways and local sites for Ti enrichment.
generation.mechanism: Due to its relatively high mobility along the grain boundaries, Ti diffuses rapidly and oxidizes to form TiO2 islands early in the oxidation process. In an oxygen-rich environment these TiO2 patches interrupt the formation of a continuous and adherent Cr2O3/Al2O3 protective scale, promoting scale spallation and localized degradation. Under reducing conditions, the limited supply of oxygen prevents full development of protective Cr/Al oxides, leading to internal oxidation along the same preferential pathways and further compromising the matrix integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a uniformly oxidized baseline, samples from the as-manufactured (high grain-boundary segregation) condition will show evidence of discontinuous oxide scales with TiO2 concentrations at grain boundaries, greater surface spallation (under oxidizing conditions), and enhanced internal oxidation (under reducing conditions). Annealed samples with reduced grain-boundary segregation should form a more uniform protective oxide scale, resulting in slower degradation rates.
generation.baseline: The as‐manufactured additively produced Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with its native microstructure and no post-processing modification.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate at temperatures between 850 and 1000 °C where grain-boundary diffusion is significant, and under gas environments that are clearly either oxygen-rich or reducing; deviations outside these ranges may activate other degradation processes.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., PMC11169556::web::016::results_and_discussion and PMC13208696::web::025::3_6_high_temperature_oxidation_mechanism) support the importance of fast diffusion along grain boundaries and the role of protective oxide formation, the specific diffusion coefficients and segregation behavior of Ti in this AM alloy remain uncertain. In addition, the net effect of the low Al content in synergy with Ti oxidation under varying atmospheres is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens: one in the as-manufactured state and one post-annealed to reduce grain-boundary segregation. Expose both sets to 900 °C for 100 h under (a) oxygen-rich atmosphere and (b) a reducing gas mixture. Characterize the oxide scales using high resolution TEM, APT, and XRD to map Ti, Cr, and Al distribution and assess oxide continuity. Additionally, perform cyclic thermal oxidation tests and measure mass gain/loss as well as spallation behavior.
measurements: Spatial distribution and concentration of TiO2 vs Cr2O3/Al2O3 in the oxide scale (TEM, APT)
Continuity/adherence of the oxide scale (XRD, scratch adhesion tests)
Mass change (thermogravimetric analysis) and spallation area quantification
Mechanical integrity (microhardness and tensile tests post-exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both as-manufactured and annealed samples exhibit similar, continuous protective oxide scales with no significant enrichment of TiO2 at grain boundaries (and similar degradation profiles) in both oxidizing and reducing conditions, then the proposed mechanism—in which differential grain-boundary diffusion of Ti governs degradation—would be invalidated.

It is important to note that the superior oxidation resistance of the Innovation Alloy stems from the synergistic effect of both its chemical composition and its unique nanocrystalline microstructure. While the Base and Synergy Alloys were prepared by conventional casting, the Innovation Alloy was fabricated via laser cladding. The rapid solidification inherent in laser cladding leads to significant grain refinement, providing a high density of grain boundaries that act as short-circuit diffusion paths for Al and Cr. This microstructural advantage accelerates the formation of a continuous protective scale. However, the compositional addition of trace Y provides a distinct benefit—the reactive element effect—which enhances the scale/alloy interfacial bonding through the formation of fine Y2O3 particles. This interfacial pinning effect is independent of the grain size and is crucial for preventing scale spallation during thermal exposure. Therefore, the Innovation Alloy represents an optimized system where both process-induced microstructural refinement and alloying-induced chemical stability work in tandem.

AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
